Polariscope

Words: 31
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An instrument with a polarizer and an optical analyzer, often with a specimen between them, used to reveal changes of polarization through transmitted intensity. Crossed ideal elements give extinction without a polarization-changing sample.

Spectroscope

Words: 9
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An instrument for observing a spectrum, including an absorption spectrum.

Spectroradiometer

Words: 31
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An instrument measuring a radiometric quantity as a function of wavelength under a stated collection geometry and calibration. Measurement at the relevant viewpoint helps connect scene or display output to observer input.

Phase shifter (P(ϕ)=diag(1,eiϕ))

Words: 42
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An optical element that adds a controlled wave phase to one path. On two path states, an ideal lossless phase shifter has the displayed unitary matrix. It changes their relative phase while leaving individual path probabilities unchanged; subsequent interference can turn that phase into an output-intensity change.

Electro-optic modulator

Words: 35
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
A device uses an applied electric field to change an optical medium's refractive index and hence the phase, amplitude or polarization of light. A phase change followed by suitable polarization analysis can provide an intensity transmission gate for active mode locking.

Pockels cell

Words: 27
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An electro-optic element whose birefringent retardance changes approximately linearly with applied voltage. Combined with a polarizer, it converts voltage-controlled polarization changes into variable optical loss for active Q-switching.

Pentaprism

Words: 58
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
A pentaprism redirects a beam through a right angle using two reflecting faces whose planes meet at 45∘. In the meridional section their combined action is a 90∘ rotation, preserving the relevant image-top direction as the beam turns. It does not by itself perform the additional lateral reversal of a roof pentaprism; the latter has an extra reflecting face.

Optical instrument OurBigBook.com

Optical cavity

Words: 477 Articles: 7
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An optical cavity supports optical fields whose phases and spatial profiles reproduce themselves after a round trip through its reflecting or guiding elements. Its resonance conditions include propagation and reflection phases. A cavity bounded by two plane mirrors is a simple example; Fabry–Pérot resonance spacing describes the frequency intervals of an ideal two-mirror arrangement.

Symmetric concave-mirror resonator (0<L<2R)

Words: 78
Optical cavity OurBigBook.com
Two identical concave mirrors of curvature radius R separated by L have half-round-trip ray matrix A=(1−2/R​L1−2L/R​). Its determinant is one and its trace is 2(1−L/R). The eigenvalues are a conjugate unit-modulus pair for the displayed interval. At the confocal point L=R, A2=−I, so it is bounded despite the full-round-trip trace reaching minus two. Matching a Gaussian beam's mirror wavefront gives zR2​=(L/2)(R−L/2) and πw02​=λzR​. The endpoints are degenerate limiting geometries, not finite confined Gaussian modes.

Longitudinal cavity mode (Δν=c/(2L))

Words: 57
Optical cavity OurBigBook.com
A normal mode whose longitudinal phase satisfies the resonator's round-trip condition. Holding the transverse mode fixed, an empty nondispersive two-mirror cavity of length L has adjacent optical frequencies separated by c/(2L). An offset from mirror or transverse phases changes the position of the mode sequence without changing this ideal spacing. A dispersive cavity instead uses its round-trip group delay.

Confocal optical resonator

Words: 102 Articles: 1
Optical cavity OurBigBook.com
A symmetric confocal optical resonator has two concave mirrors of equal curvature R, separated by R. Its symmetric fundamental Gaussian beam has a central beam waist and Rayleigh range R/2. Its ideal transverse spectrum has degeneracies, so transmission at one resonance need not certify exclusive excitation of the fundamental normal mode.

Confocal reciprocal-Rayleigh-range map (zR​zR′​=(L/2)2)

Words: 58
Confocal optical resonator OurBigBook.com
For two equal mirrors of radius L separated by L, a Gaussian waist at the centre is reflected to another waist at the same plane. Putting a=L/2, the mirror maps q=a+izR​ to −a+ia2/zR​, so the reflected Rayleigh range is a2/zR​. Both beams have equal spots on the mirrors although their waist radii differ. Equal waist sizes select zR​=L/2.

Optical mode matching

Words: 60
Optical cavity OurBigBook.com
Optical mode matching makes the spatial field of an incident beam equal to a desired optical cavity normal mode. For fundamental circular Gaussian beams, matching the complex beam parameter fixes the beam waist size and location; the optical axis, polarization and frequency must also match. A single converging optical lens connects waist Rayleigh ranges zA​,zB​ only when f2≥zA​zB​. With s=f2/(zA​zB​)−1​, waist-to-lens distances obey u=f±zA​s, v=f±zB​s with correlated signs, followed by physical distance constraints.

Photon lifetime (τc​)

Words: 50
Optical cavity OurBigBook.com
The photon lifetime is the exponential decay time of stored energy in an unpumped optical cavity. If a round trip of duration T retains an energy fraction ρ, then τc​=−T/logρ and the quality factor is Q=ωτc​. Field-amplitude decay takes twice this time. Output coupling contributes to the loss as well as absorption and scattering.

Lorentz invariance of optical cavity resonance

Words: 81
Optical cavity OurBigBook.com
A Lorentz transformation of a resonant optical cavity transforms both the electromagnetic field and the mirror worldlines. Boundary conditions and event-by-event phase matching remain satisfied. For a longitudinal boost, a cavity of rest length L has length L/γ and unequal forward/backward frequencies γω0​(1∓β). The coordinate round-trip time is 2γL/c, while the phase rate on a moving mirror is ω0​/γ, so the round-trip phase is still 2ω0​L/c. A stationary-mirror resonance formula with only length contraction inserted describes the wrong boundary-value problem.

Mirror

Words: 154 Articles: 3
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
A mirror redirects light according to the law of reflection. Its orientation determines the reflected beam direction in an interferometer.

Parabolic reflector

Words: 33
Mirror OurBigBook.com
A parabolic reflector has a paraboloidal reflecting surface. The law of reflection makes all incident light rays parallel to its optical axis pass through one focus in ideal geometrical optics. This removes on-axis spherical aberration and explains its use as a receiving antenna for distant sources.

Concave spherical mirror (f=R/2)

Words: 43
Mirror OurBigBook.com
A concave spherical mirror reflects at the inside of a spherical surface of radius of curvature R. For incident light rays near its optical axis, the law of reflection gives paraxial focal length f=R/2. Rays farther from the optical axis have different axial crossing positions, causing spherical aberration; one must specify a criterion to define the best full-aperture focus.

Plane mirror

Words: 62
Mirror OurBigBook.com
A plane mirror has a flat reflecting surface. The law of reflection sends incident unit direction d to d−2(d⋅n)n, where n is its unit normal. It forms a virtual image of an object the same perpendicular distance behind the reflecting plane as the object is in front. Two successive plane mirrors whose planes meet at angle γ rotate the ray geometry through 2γ about their intersection.

Grism

Words: 8
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An optical component combining an optical prism and a diffraction grating.

Camera lucida

Words: 21
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
A camera lucida superposes the apparent image of an object on a drawing surface, allowing microscope positions to be marked by hand.

Optical filter

Words: 19 Articles: 1
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An optical filter selectively transmits light according to properties such as wavelength or polarization of waves.

Interference filter

Words: 9
Optical filter OurBigBook.com
An optical filter that uses interference to select a band of wavelengths.

Goniometer

Words: 5
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An instrument for measuring angles.

Focal ratio (F=f/D)

Words: 512
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
The focal ratio, or f-number, of a converging optical instrument focused at infinity is the dimensionless quantity
N=F=Df​,
(1)
where f>0 is effective focal length and D is the on-axis entrance pupil diameter. The notation f/4 means N=4, not f=4 in a particular unit. A 100mm focal length with D=25mm gives f/4. Closing the aperture stop until D=12.5mm gives f/8 while retaining the same focal length. The mechanical opening need not equal D. [ref].
For a thin lens in air with a circular aperture stop at the thin lens, the converging bundle from a distant on-axis point has half-angle α satisfying
tanα=2fD​=2N1​,α≃2N1​in radians.
(2)
The last step uses the small-angle approximation. For a compound optical lens, the cone is set by the image-side optical pupil and its distance from the receiving plane; the simple triangle is not an exact high-angle rule. At finite object distance a thin lens instead gives v=f(1+∣m∣), by its imaging equation and transverse magnification, so its working cone corresponds to v/D=N(1+∣m∣). Nominal focal ratio therefore does not alone specify close-range image irradiance. [ref].
Two useful scalings follow under stated conditions. For a fixed uniform incident beam and unchanged transmission, collected radiant flux scales as D2. For an extended source with fixed radiance, the central image irradiance scales approximately as N−2 in the paraxial approximation: the solid angle of the cone scales as (D/f)2. For an ideal uniformly illuminated unobscured circular entrance pupil, the first dark ring of the point spread function has angular radius and focal plane radius
θ1​≃1.22Dλ​,r1​≃fθ1​=1.22λN.
(3)
Here λ is wavelength. These are first-zero radii, not diameters or a universal rule for resolving arbitrary objects. A proof outline evaluates the circular aperture's Fraunhofer diffraction using its Fourier transform, then uses the first zero of the resulting Bessel function. [ref].
At λ=0.55μm, the example's f/4 and f/8 first-ring radii are 2.684 and 5.368μm. Closing the aperture stop halves D, quarters collected radiant flux and doubles this diffraction radius. It can also reduce optical aberrations by excluding outer light rays; actual sharpness reflects both effects. This explains why a smaller aperture need not produce a sharper image. [ref].
A proposed optical bench check puts a fixed collimator before a converging thin lens and a photodetector large enough to collect the entire image behind it. Compare two centred aperture stops of known diameters while fixing source output, detector gain and integration time. The integrated signal tests the D2 collection law; a spatially resolved optical camera at the focal plane can separately measure the point spread function. Repeat a dark reading and the first aperture stop, and check that neither the incoming beam nor detector clips either bundle. A resolved pinhole source, imperfect collimation, optical aberrations and detector pixel size can dominate the apparent spot width; a single peak reading does not measure total collected radiant flux.

Optical camera

Words: 18
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An optical camera images incident beams on a photodetector; a spectrograph optical camera maps a diffracted direction into a position in its focal plane.

Optical slit

Words: 24
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An optical slit selects a narrow region of a focal plane. In a slit-limited spectrograph, the width of its image divided by the linear spectral dispersion sets the spectral width.

Focal plane

Words: 73 Articles: 1
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
A focal plane is a plane in which an optical system forms images of distant directions. Aberrations can make the best-focus surface curved; a flat detector may then require a field-flattening optical element.

Back focal plane

Words: 40
Focal plane OurBigBook.com
The plane one focal length beyond a lens. In a paraxial imaging system, incident parallel rays of a given direction focus at one point in this plane; it is therefore an angular or diffraction plane distinct from a finite-distance object's image plane.

High-contrast imaging

Words: 131 Articles: 3
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
High-contrast imaging seeks faint objects near a bright source. Residual point spread functions and speckle patterns can dominate photon shot noise; angular differential imaging and simultaneous spectral differential imaging use source motion or spectral diversity to distinguish them.

Differential-imaging self-subtraction

Words: 40
High-contrast imaging OurBigBook.com
A companion or extended source contributes to the stellar reference used in differential imaging. Subtracting that reference removes part of the desired signal and distorts its shape, photometry or astrometry. Artificial-source injection and forward modelling can estimate the throughput loss.

Simultaneous spectral differential imaging

Words: 35
High-contrast imaging OurBigBook.com
Simultaneous spectral differential imaging compares images in nearby bands, rescaled so stellar speckle patterns approximately coincide. A companion has a different positional or spectral response. Simultaneity reduces temporal variation but does not remove chromatic and non-common-path errors.

Angular differential imaging

Words: 32
High-contrast imaging OurBigBook.com
Angular differential imaging keeps the instrument pupil fixed while the sky rotates. A stellar reference point spread function is subtracted, then the residuals are derotated and combined. Insufficient rotation and imperfect reference selection cause differential-imaging self-subtraction.

Fabry–Pérot interferometer

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
A Fabry–Pérot interferometer uses repeated specular reflections between two nearly parallel, partially transmitting surfaces. Its transmitted light is the sum of contributions that have made zero, one, two, or more additional round trips. Their complex amplitudes reinforce only near particular wave phases, producing narrow transmission peaks that select wavelength intervals. Scanning the spacing or angle of incidence can build an imaging spectral cube: an image at each selected wavelength.
The surprising feature is that highly reflecting mirrors can together transmit all the incident power at resonance in the ideal symmetric, lossless model. Each individual contribution is weak, but many contributions arrive in phase. Between resonances the same contributions cancel strongly. Increasing mirror reflectivity sharpens the peaks instead of simply suppressing every transmitted signal; finesse quantifies that selectivity. An optical spectrum with nearby spectral lines can therefore produce distinguishable peaks, provided their separation is large enough relative to the instrument's peak width and their orders are identified.
Charles Fabry and Alfred Perot developed the instrument together; Optica dates its development from 1896 to 1898.[ref]

Absorbing Fabry–Pérot mirror phase and transmission (δ=4πνnd/c+2argr)

Words: 63
Fabry–Pérot interferometer OurBigBook.com
For identical mirrors with power reflectivity R, transmission T and absorption 1−R−T, summing round trips at normal incidence gives
I0​It​​=(1−R)2+4Rsin2(δ/2)T2​.
(4)
Here δ includes propagation and both internal reflection phases. Optical absorption reduces the resonant peak below unity, while a nonzero reflection phase shifts the resonance condition δ=2πm. Frequency-dependent mirror phase and refractive index can also change the free spectral range.

Order-safe angular scanning of a Fabry–Pérot spectrum

Words: 68
Fabry–Pérot interferometer OurBigBook.com
Spectral resolution and order identification are separate design constraints. An instrumental width narrower than a line separation does not prevent a different interference order from placing another wavelength at the same angle. Choose optical thickness so the source range fits a known order interval, sufficient finesse to resolve neighbouring lines, and an angular window or order-sorting filter to exclude unwanted orders. Material dispersion and the internal/external angle conversion must be calibrated.

Air-gap optical path difference in a Fabry–Pérot interferometer (Δ=2dcosθ)

Words: 45
Fabry–Pérot interferometer OurBigBook.com
For an air gap of thickness d, an extra internal round trip has length 2d/cosθ, but consecutive transmitted rays emerge at different positions. Comparing them at the same outgoing wavefront subtracts 2dtanθsinθ, leaving optical path difference 2dcosθ. Reflection-coating wave phases are separate from this geometric path calculation.

Fabry–Pérot transmission from multiple reflections (T(δ)=[1+4R(1−R)−2sin2(δ/2)]−1)

Words: 564
Fabry–Pérot interferometer OurBigBook.com
Consider two identical, lossless parallel mirrors with intensity reflectivity 0≤R<1, separation d, and a uniform transparent medium of refractive index n. Fix one polarization of an electromagnetic wave and an internal angle of incidence θ measured from the mirror normal vector. Illuminate with a monochromatic wave having planar wavefronts; the emerging contributions must overlap coherently in the detected direction. Define T=Itransmitted​/Iincident​ using the same incident and exit media. Each mirror transmits a fraction 1−R of incident power. Its reflected wave amplitude has magnitude R​, so two internal specular reflections multiply the circulating complex amplitude by magnitude R, not R2.
Let λ be the vacuum wavelength and choose the reflection wave phase convention in which the product of the two internal amplitude reflection coefficients is real and positive. The phase difference between successive transmitted contributions, evaluated on a common outgoing wavefront, is
δ=λ4πndcosθ​.
(5)
With other mirror coatings or phase conventions, use the total δ=4πndcosθ/λ+ϕrt​, where ϕrt​ is the sum of the two internal reflection wave phases. The stated resonance positions presume ϕrt​=0 modulo 2π; a constant nonzero ϕrt​ shifts them, while a frequency-dependent one can also change their spacing.
Why does the cosine appear rather than its reciprocal? Inside the gap, the extra two legs have optical path length 2nd/cosθ. But the later emerging contribution starts 2dtanθ farther along the mirror. Comparing both on one outgoing wavefront subtracts 2ndtanθsinθ from that path difference, leaving 2ndcosθ. Equivalently, a plane wave's mirror-normal wavevector component is kz​=(2πn/λ)cosθ, so the round-trip wave phase is 2kz​d. The diagram uses the same medium outside and inside to show the common-wavefront subtraction directly; at a refracting exit interface, tangential wavevector matching in Snell's law supplies the same result.
Absorb the common first-pass wave phase into the incident complex amplitude Ein​. Successive transmitted contributions are (1−R)Ein​, (1−R)Ein​Reiδ, and so on. The superposition principle and the convergent geometric series give
Ein​Eout​​=(1−R)∑j=0∞​Rjeijδ=1−Reiδ1−R​,T=​Ein​Eout​​​2=(1−R)2+4Rsin2(δ/2)(1−R)2​.
(6)
The last step expands the squared complex modulus as 1+R2−2Rcosδ. This transmission profile is often called the Airy transmission function; it is distinct from the Airy disk, a diffraction image of a circular aperture. The University of Washington's lab handout gives the same transmission profile and distinguishes mirror reflectivity from other sources of peak broadening.[ref]
For an original example, set R=3/4. At δ=0, the amplitudes add to (1/4)/(1−3/4)=1, so T=1. At δ=π, they alternate in sign and add to (1/4)/(1+3/4)=1/7, so T=1/49. At δ=π/2, the amplitude is 4/25+3i/25 and T=1/25. Adding the individual intensities instead would give (1−R)2∑j​R2j=(1−R)/(1+R)=1/7, independent of wave phase; that discards the wave interference responsible for the peaks.
In general the maximum is Tmax​=1 at δ=2πm, with integer m, and the minimum is Tmin​=[(1−R)/(1+R)]2 halfway between peaks. Perfect resonant transmission requires identical lossless mirrors, coherent illumination, and sufficient time to establish the steady field. Absorption, unequal mirror transmission, finite beams that fail to overlap, and fluctuations of d can reduce it. The exactly reflecting case R=1 is excluded: no incident power enters through a perfectly reflecting mirror, and the resonant limit R→1− is singular.

Fabry–Pérot interferometer OurBigBook.com
At normal incidence, with no optical dispersion and zero round-trip reflection wave phase modulo 2π, the resonance condition in Fabry–Pérot transmission from multiple reflections is
2nd=mλm​,νm​=2ndmc​,ΔνFSR​=νm+1​−νm​=2ndc​.
(7)
Here ν is frequency and c is the speed of light in vacuum. A change of ν by one free spectral range advances the round-trip wave phase by 2π. At fixed internal angle of incidence θ, the same nondispersive model gives c/(2ndcosθ). Holding the external angle of incidence fixed in a dispersive medium need not hold the internal θ fixed, because of Snell's law.
For stipulated n=1 and d=10mm, the free spectral range is 14.9896229GHz using c=299792458ms−1. A frequency difference of 0.10ΔνFSR​ is therefore 1.49896229GHz. Transmission repeats every free spectral range: one isolated scan cannot distinguish that separation from 1.10ΔνFSR​. Independent knowledge of the optical spectrum, an additional filter, or a changed mirror separation is needed to assign orders.
Equal spacing in frequency does not imply equal spacing in wavelength. At normal incidence the exact adjacent resonance wavelengths obey
λm​−λm+1​=m(m+1)2nd​=m+1λm​​≃2ndλm2​​(m≫1).
(8)
For example, choosing 2nd=10λ10​ makes the exact gap to order 11 equal to λ10​/11, while the high-order estimate gives λ10​/10. The approximation is already ten percent larger at order 10. With optical dispersion or frequency-dependent reflection wave phase, obtain local spacings from the total phase difference instead: Δν≃2π/(dδ/dν) when its derivative varies little over one order.

The finesse of a Fabry–Pérot interferometer is its free spectral range divided by a transmission peak's full width at half maximum. Large finesse means a narrow accepted frequency interval compared with the spacing between repeated orders. Here half maximum means T=1/2 of the ideal unit peak, with zero detector background subtracted; it does not mean halfway between the transmission minimum and maximum.
Write A=4R/(1−R)2 for the coefficient multiplying sin2(δ/2) in Fabry–Pérot transmission from multiple reflections. This coefficient is sometimes called the coefficient of finesse; it is not the finesse F. About a resonance δ=2πm, put ϵ=δ−2πm. Solving T=1/2 gives
sin2(ϵ/2)=A1​,ΔδFWHM​=4arcsin(2R​1−R​),
(9)
and, since one free spectral range advances the wave phase by 2π,
ΔνFSR​ΔνFWHM​​=π2​arcsin(2R​1−R​),F=2arcsin[(1−R)/(2R​)]π​.
(10)
These are exact for the ideal nondispersive model with constant R and linear frequency dependence of δ. The inverse sine requires (1−R)/(2R​)≤1, or R≥3−22​≃0.171573. At equality, neighbouring peaks merely touch half maximum at their shared minima: the nominal width is one full free spectral range and F=1. Isolated half-maximum peaks require the strict inequality. Below this threshold the transmission never falls to 1/2, so this peak-width definition supplies no finesse; at R=0 the transmission is flat.
For large reflectivity, the small-angle approximation arcsinx≃x gives
F≃1−RπR​​,ΔνFSR​ΔνFWHM​​≃πR​1−R​.
(11)
This is a high-reflectivity approximation, not an identity for every R. The original dimensionless examples below have exact full width at half maximum values obtained from the inverse sine formula.

For the stipulated 10mm vacuum gap, R=0.95 gives an ideal full width at half maximum of about 244.792MHz. This instrumental width is not a measured spectral line width. A real scan also depends on the source profile, accepted angles, mirror shape, alignment, and scan stability. The University of Washington handout separately discusses mirror-reflectivity, mirror-flatness, and detector-pinhole contributions; increasing R alone cannot remove the others.[ref]

To separate a pair of lines spaced by Δν by at least M peak widths, require dF≥Mc/(2Δν). Putting both lines inside one unambiguous free spectral range additionally requires d<c/(2Δν), so F>M. In terms of their vacuum wavelengths, c/Δν=λ1​λ2​/∣λ2​−λ1​∣.
The strict order condition needs a margin if tails from adjacent periodic peaks are to be negligible. If every neighbouring peak in a scanned two-line periodic spectrum must be separated by M widths, the stronger condition is min(Δν,νFSR​−Δν)≥MνFSR​/F. Ordinary resolving power alone does not prevent ambiguous repeated orders. A fixed etalon's transmission as a function of wavelength is a periodic-in-frequency filter; it is not automatically a plot of the incident source's spectral lines.

Scanning Fabry–Pérot measurement

Fabry–Pérot interferometer OurBigBook.com
An actual teaching experiment in LM-0300 Fabry Perot Spectrum Analyser by Walter Luhs, §§3.1.1–3.1.2, prepares a green laser beam by aligning it near and far along a rail, then centring back-reflected light from adjustable curved mirrors. An actuator using piezoelectricity moves one mirror. A screen first displays interference fringes; a focusing optical lens and photodiode then replace the viewing arrangement. The oscilloscope records the photodiode signal and the piezo drive reference on separate channels, using the latter as its trigger. Alignment and mirror separation are adjusted to suppress extra transverse normal modes; source temperature and drive electric current are controlled. Repeated peaks calibrate the scan using the appropriate free spectral range, and their spacing divided by their full width at half maximum estimates finesse.[ref]
This experiment uses a confocal curved-mirror cavity, whose repeated peak families can have spacing c/(4d) in air; it must not be calibrated blindly with the parallel-mirror c/(2d). Extra transverse normal modes can mimic source features. A finite measured peak width bounds source sharpness only after instrumental broadening is considered; it does not determine the source's intrinsic width by itself.[ref]
For an independent ideal scan calculation, hold a narrow laser wavelength fixed and vary the parallel-mirror gap d at normal incidence. Advancing one resonance order requires Δd=λ/(2n). If d changes uniformly over the measured interval, the time between repeated peaks divided by their full width at half maximum in time equals finesse. The cancellation of scan rate follows from d(t)=d0​+vt: both peak spacing and peak width are divided by the same ∣v∣. It fails if the scan rate changes appreciably over that interval. A practical control in the University of Washington's motor-driven flat-mirror experiment is to check that successive peaks are equally spaced before using the time axis this way; its handout also warns that table strain and aggressive low-pass filtering alter the trace.[ref]

Beam splitter

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
A beam splitter is an optical instrument that routes an incident beam of light into transmitted and reflected beams. It also combines incident complex amplitudes: two inputs can contribute to the same output. A common geometry has four optical ports, with two chosen as inputs and two as outputs. A beam splitter changes the field; a photodetector supplies a measurement.[ref]
For one illuminated input of a passive beam splitter, at specified wavelength, angle of incidence and electromagnetic polarization, define power transmittance T=Ptransmitted​/Pin​, reflectance R=Preflected​/Pin​ and radiometric absorptance A=Pabsorbed​/Pin​. In steady operation, with no gain or other source, no net stored energy change, and all escaping light included in the transmitted or reflected collection,
T+R+A=1.
(12)
This is conservation of energy divided by incident power. If T and R count only the intended output beams, include a separate scattered or otherwise uncollected fraction L: then T+R+A+L=1. Missing output power need not be wave absorption. For an original specified example, Pin​=10mW, T=0.45, R=0.50 and A=0.05 give 4.5mW transmitted, 5.0mW reflected and 0.5mW absorbed; these are assumed values, not measurements.
A 50:50 beam splitter specifies equal output powers for one input, not equal complex amplitudes without a relative wave phase. Recombination needs the beam splitter scattering matrix, including its wave phases. A nonpolarizing beam splitter approximately divides both orthogonal linear polarizations in the same power ratio over its specified operating range; a polarizing beam splitter deliberately routes the two differently.
The useful surprise is that the same component divides power with one input and steers power by wave interference with two inputs. In a Michelson interferometer or Mach-Zehnder interferometer, mirror motion changes relative wave phase, turning a small change in optical path length into a measurable change in output power.

Reversing propagation changes the input/output assignment. Four geometrical connections do not imply four independent input complex amplitudes in the chosen two-input configuration.

Beam splitter OurBigBook.com
For a linear, fixed-frequency beam splitter, choose power-normalized complex amplitudes a1​,a2​ at its input optical ports and b1​,b2​ at its output optical ports: ∣aj​∣2 and ∣bj​∣2 are powers. The scalar description treats one specified electromagnetic polarization and matching transverse profiles; other fields require additional components. With the geometrical ordering in the diagram,
(b1​b2​​)=S(a1​a2​​),S=(tr​r′t′​).
(13)
Here t,t′ are transmission complex amplitudes per unit input and r,r′ are reflection complex amplitudes per unit input. In this power normalization, a single input gives T=∣t∣2 and R=∣r∣2. Raw electric field amplitudes in different media generally need additional power-normalization factors.
If these two output optical ports account for all outgoing power and the device has no loss or gain, S is a unitary matrix:
S†S=I,∣t∣2+∣r∣2=∣r′∣2+∣t′∣2=1,t∗r′+r∗t′=0.
(14)
The dagger is the Hermitian transpose and a star is complex conjugation. To prove the condition, substitute b=Sa into conservation of total power for every input vector: a†(S†S−I)a=0. Inputs (1,0) and (0,1) fix the diagonal entries; (1,1) and (1,i) fix the real and imaginary parts of the off-diagonal entry. A lossy two-output description instead has S†S≤I for a passive device.[ref]
One consistent ideal symmetric 50:50 choice is
S=2​1​(1i​i1​),b1​=2​a1​+ia2​​,b2​=2​ia1​+a2​​.
(15)
Each reflection carries +π/2 relative wave phase in this convention. The columns have unit vector norm and zero inner product, directly verifying that S is a unitary matrix. Choosing a different phase convention for complex amplitudes at the optical ports replaces S by Dout​SDin−1​, where the D are diagonal matrices whose entries have modulus one; the input complex amplitudes must be transformed consistently. Observable powers are unchanged. The displayed i is a convention for this ideal model, not a universal reflection rule for every coating or incidence geometry.

Beam splitter OurBigBook.com
Suppose the two input beams share frequency, electromagnetic polarization and overlapping transverse profiles at each output, with stable relative wave phase during the photodetector's averaging interval. For the ideal beam splitter scattering matrix above, expanding the squared complex amplitudes gives
P1​=2∣a1​∣2+∣a2​∣2​−Im(a1∗​a2​),P2​=2∣a1​∣2+∣a2​∣2​+Im(a1∗​a2​).
(17)
The imaginary part terms describe wave interference. Applying the single-input power split to each input separately and adding the results would discard these terms. Their opposite signs ensure P1​+P2​=∣a1​∣2+∣a2​∣2: conservation of energy survives even when one output is dark.
For an original example, let a1​=P​, a2​=P​eiδ and P=1mW. Then P1​=P(1−sinδ) and P2​=P(1+sinδ):
Relative input wave phase δOutput power P1​Output power P2​
01mW1mW
+π/202mW
−π/22mW0
At +π/2, a2​=iP​ makes b1​=(P​−P​)/2​=0 and b2​=i2P​; at −π/2 the dark output swaps. Thus the two inputs can feed all their combined power into one output without gain. At zero relative input wave phase, the splitter's own relative wave phase leaves the contributions in quadrature, so neither output is dark.
For fluctuating fields, average the cross term as Im⟨a1∗​a2​⟩. It vanishes for mutually uncorrelated inputs, making the independent power-splitting rule valid for the averaged output. Partial first-order optical coherence reduces it. Orthogonal linear polarizations eliminate the cross term in a polarization-insensitive power readout, and spatial mismatch reduces the overlap. Detector averaging can also erase rapid relative wave phase changes. A fixed relation between two inputs can be prepared by splitting one laser beam and recombining the two arms.
An actual teaching protocol in Michelson Interferometer & Precision Wavelength Measurement — Week 1, University of Colorado Boulder, §§4–6, starts with an ideal-model prediction, then builds a Michelson interferometer using a helium-neon laser, a nonpolarizing beam splitter, adjustable mirrors, a micrometer translation stage and a photodetector. Steering mirrors align beam overlap at near and far planes; far-plane interference fringes refine alignment. Moving the arm mirror changes the returning relative wave phase; detector voltage is watched with a live acquisition display or oscilloscope. The guide compares measured arm powers with 50:50 splitting and asks for a revised field model. It tests electromagnetic polarization dependence, optionally changing one arm with a quarter-wave plate, and estimates noise from repeated readings at fixed mirror position. These controls test whether fringe changes reflect coherent recombination rather than splitter imbalance or misalignment. The guide supplies a protocol, not a numerical dataset. Its detector noise, imperfect overlap and electromagnetic polarization mismatch limit displacement inference.[ref]
Additional background subtraction controls follow from the field model: block both arms to record the detector offset and ambient light, then unblock each arm separately to establish its detected power at fixed gain. With both open, scan the mirror and compare extrema after subtracting that background. Keep the detector below saturation and repeat the scan to check drift. A changing signal alone cannot distinguish source optical coherence from motion or changing overlap. For a vacuum round trip, a mirror displacement x changes relative wave phase by 4πx/λ; the useful signal is its modulation after detection, not an optical-frequency oscillation that the detector must resolve.

Nonpolarizing beam splitter

Words: 51
Beam splitter OurBigBook.com
A nonpolarizing beam splitter is designed for approximately equal power splitting ratios for the two orthogonal linear polarizations, at specified wavelengths and angle of incidence. It need not be 50:50, lossless, or have equal transmission and reflection wave phases for both linear polarizations. A scalar beam splitter scattering matrix therefore still requires a specified electromagnetic polarization and operating range. Polarizing beam splitters instead aim to separate those linear polarizations into different paths.

Polarizing beam splitter

Words: 235
Beam splitter OurBigBook.com
A polarizing beam splitter sends two orthogonal linear polarizations to different output paths. Acting coherently on α∣H⟩+β∣V⟩, it correlates path with photon polarization instead of measuring photon polarization unless a path is actually detected or discarded.
For an ideal polarizing beam splitter with one input, choose orthogonal unit electromagnetic polarization vectors eH​,eV​ and an incident power-normalized field aH​eH​+aV​eV​. If H is transmitted and V reflected, the output powers are Ptransmitted​=∣aH​∣2 and Preflected​=∣aV​∣2. The associated complex amplitudes can acquire different wave phases; the routing is not an equal-power split for every incident electromagnetic polarization. For linear polarization at angle θ to H, input power P gives Pcos2θ and Psin2θ, respectively. At θ=30∘, a stipulated 4mW input gives 3mW transmitted and 1mW reflected. A 45∘ input gives equal powers even though an H input goes entirely into the transmitted output.[ref]
Real polarizing beam splitters have leakage into the unwanted output and losses. Each linear polarization has its own field transformation and power coefficients. To make an ordinary power wave interference term between the two output contributions, first bring them into the same path with overlapping transverse profiles and a common electromagnetic polarization, for example using a polarizer. Merely placing two orthogonal linear polarizations on a polarization-insensitive photodetector adds their powers. Coherent routing can be reversed by suitable optics before detection; discarding a path loses access to that part of the field but supplies no recorded measurement outcome by itself.

Field of view

Words: 484
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
The field of view is the region of object directions sampled by an optical instrument in one pointing. State whether it is horizontal, vertical or diagonal, and whether it is a full angle or a half-angle. An object-plane width in millimetres also describes a field of view, but requires a specified object distance. Neither that width nor the angular field of view is the aperture diameter or the diffraction-limited resolution.
For a centred flat rectangular photodetector of width w in the focal plane, with positive effective focal length f, infinity focus and ideal rectilinear imaging without optical distortion, the full horizontal field of view is
Θx​=2arctan(2fw​).
(19)
The model maps an object direction θ to image height of magnitude ∣y∣=f∣tanθ∣; set ∣y∣=w/2 and use the inverse tangent. This retains exact right triangle geometry within the stipulated imaging model; a paraxial focal length alone does not guarantee that a real wide-field optical lens obeys it. With detector height h, replace w by h for the vertical field of view, and by w2+h2​ for the diagonal field of view. The small-angle approximation gives Θx​≃w/f in radians. [ref].
For an original worked example, a 36mm detector width gives Θx​≈39.60∘ at f=50mm, and 20.41∘ at f=100mm. Keeping D=25mm makes these f/2 and f/4 respectively: the field of view changes because f changes. By contrast, closing D from 25 to 12.5mm at f=100mm changes f/4 to f/8 while retaining 20.41∘ in this model. The clean separation is useful: entrance pupil area controls collection, focal ratio controls the paraxial cone, and w/f controls angular image coverage. Edge clipping, optical distortion, field curvature and optical aberrations can restrict the practically usable field of view.
A proposed angular readout on an optical bench illuminates a small asymmetric target at the optical focus of a collimator, providing a bundle with a known direction. Rotate the optical camera about the centre of its entrance pupil, reading a graduated rotation stage, and record the target image position on its fixed photodetector. Centre the target to establish zero; turn left and right until its centre reaches each detector edge. The difference between stage readings measures the full horizontal field of view. Repeat with a smaller aperture stop: unchanged edge directions but reduced signal support the distinction between collection and angular coverage. Keep the same active detector width, infinity focus, illumination, integration time and gain; approach each reading from the same direction to check mechanical backlash. A finite target blurs the edge criterion, detector thresholds can imitate lost coverage, and a wide bundle must illuminate the whole entrance pupil at every tested angle. These checks distinguish a geometrical boundary from insufficient signal. The analytical diagram is the prediction for this protocol, not a record of its execution.

The attraction of an optical microscope is that seeing can become measuring: a stage micrometer supplies a known object-space length, and microscope scale calibration converts an image readout into a specimen length. This also separates a large-looking image from a trustworthy size estimate. Meanwhile, diffraction-limited resolution depends on numerical aperture and wavelength; empty magnification enlarges an existing blur without revealing additional structure.

The viewing optical lens assembly that acts as a magnifier of the intermediate microscope image. With that image at its front focal plane, the outgoing light rays from each point are parallel. In the small-angle approximation, the viewed angle is hi​/fe​, versus hi​/D for the same image-sized object at reference distance D, giving Me​=D/fe​.[ref]
A finite-distance virtual image requires a different eyepiece conjugate. In the ideal thin lens model, with the eye close to the eyepiece and the virtual image at distance D, the angular magnification becomes 1+D/fe​. Intermediate microscope image

Optical microscope OurBigBook.com
The real image of the specimen supplied to the microscope eyepiece or a recording surface. In the example above, a bare detector placed at x=60mm records an image five times the specimen's length, inverted. It does not record a fifty-times image: that number compares viewing angles under the stated reference convention. An optical camera receiving the eyepiece's outgoing light needs its own optical lens to form a further real image, with a recording scale determined by that added image formation.

Finite-conjugate microscope

Words: 114
Optical microscope OurBigBook.com
An optical microscope whose microscope objective is designed to form a real image at a specified finite distance. The intended image distance and optical aberration corrections belong together; mechanical tube length is a mounting specification, not automatically the image distance measured from a principal plane.[ref]
Why can a small displacement produce a large image? For a converging thin lens, write uo​=fo​+ϵ with epsilon>0. Substitution into the thin lens equation gives
vo​=ϵfo​(fo​+ϵ)​,mo​=−ϵfo​​.
(22)
The similar triangles construction supplies the minus sign. The example has epsilon=2mm and hence mo​=−5. Letting epsilon decrease moves the real image farther away; it does not keep the microscope eyepiece in focus at a fixed position. Large transverse magnification therefore requires the correct conjugate geometry, not merely a short focal length.

Infinity-corrected microscope

Words: 158 Articles: 1
Optical microscope OurBigBook.com
An optical microscope whose microscope objective, with the specimen at its designed front focal plane, sends out a parallel bundle of light rays from each specimen point. Different specimen points generally give different bundle directions. A tube lens then forms the finite intermediate microscope image; the microscope eyepiece views it. This parallel region permits suitable optical accessories to be inserted. Finite-conjugate and infinity-corrected components must be matched to their intended system.[ref]
In the ideal paraxial approximation, an object height ho​ at objective focal length fo​ gives bundle slope −ho​/fo​. A tube lens of focal length ft​ maps that slope to hi​=−ft​ho​/fo​, so
mo​=−fo​ft​​.
(23)
This is a two-assembly result. Substituting infinity into the single-objective transverse magnification −vo​/uo​ would not describe the finite recorded image. Infinity correction concerns the region after the objective; relaxed-eye viewing concerns the region after the eyepiece. They are distinct conditions.

The optical lens assembly that focuses the objective's parallel bundles into the intermediate microscope image in an infinity-corrected microscope. Its focal length participates in the objective-system transverse magnification −ft​/fo​.

Microscope scale calibration (c=L/N)

Words: 385 Articles: 2
Optical microscope OurBigBook.com
Microscope scale calibration compares an image readout with a known specimen length. This documented practical uses an eyepiece graticule, stage micrometer and Köhler illumination. Focus the graticule; place the reference on the stage with the objective-appropriate cover glass. Focus both scales with the chosen microscope objective, then rotate and translate them into parallel alignment. Read widely separated coincidences using consistent line edges. Record the optical configuration and recalibrate for each objective.[ref]
The stage micrometer is the reference; preserve the optical configuration when substituting the specimen. Line width, focus, edge selection and optical aberrations limit accuracy. Additional recommended checks are realignment and another known interval: agreement tests repeatability and scale consistency, not absolute reference accuracy.[ref]
Here is an original toy calculation, not the source's calibration example or measured data. Suppose a reference span L=100μm coincides with N=40 eyepiece intervals. Then the calibration factor and the length corresponding to n=18 specimen intervals are
c=NL​=2.5μm per interval,ℓ=nc=45μm.
(24)
This works because both readouts use the same image-to-specimen scale: ℓ/L=n/N. One must count intervals, not tick marks; forty intervals have forty-one bounding ticks. In an ideal linear scale model, if identifying the calibration endpoints introduces a total readout error of ±1 interval, the inferred factor ranges from 100/41 to 100/39μm per interval. Holding n=18 exact gives 43.90≤ℓ/μm≤46.15. This isolates one contribution to measurement uncertainty; it is not a complete uncertainty budget or a measured confidence interval.
For a recorded real image, image a stage micrometer at the same capture settings to calibrate length per detector pixel. Resizing changes length per pixel; update the scale bar accordingly. Eye-viewing angular magnification alone supplies no digital image scale.[ref]

Empty magnification

Optical microscope OurBigBook.com
Empty magnification enlarges an image without revealing additional specimen detail. Adequate angular magnification can make existing detail visible to the eye, but it cannot undo the objective's diffraction blur. For equally bright, mutually incoherent optical point sources and an ideal circular optical pupil, a commonly used lateral Rayleigh criterion in object space is
dR​≃NA0.61λ​,NA=nsinα,
(25)
where λ is the vacuum wavelength, n is the specimen-medium refractive index, and α is the admitted half-angle. For this model, λ=550nm and NA=0.25 give dR​≃1.342μm; changing only numerical aperture to 0.50 gives 0.671μm. Changing only the eyepiece leaves this object-space scale unchanged. Illumination, optical coherence, optical aberrations and specimen visibility matter in real instruments; this criterion is not a universal threshold.[ref]
The geometric reason is especially simple. If a fixed recorded image is enlarged by a factor q>0, a feature separation s and a blur width b become qs and qb. Their ratio remains
qbqs​=bs​.
(26)
This is the lower-panel construction in the diagram. A change to the microscope objective can change numerical aperture and hence the specimen detail captured; a display zoom changes how large that captured detail looks. Microscope scale calibration, diffraction-limited resolution and angular magnification are three complementary properties to report.

Phase-contrast microscopy

Words: 911 Articles: 7
Optical microscope OurBigBook.com
Phase-contrast microscopy converts specimen-dependent phase differences into visible light intensity differences. It can reveal structures in living, unstained biological cells, allowing their changes to be followed without first making an absorbing preparation.[ref] The key question is how an optical microscope can read a phase when an ordinary detector records light intensity.
Consider a transparent specimen with complex amplitude transmission t(x,y)=eiϕ(x,y). In ideal in-focus coherent imaging with all relevant spatial frequencies transmitted, its image has I=∣t∣2=1: varying ϕ alone produces no brightness detail. This is a particular model, not a claim that all transparent specimens are invisible. Diffraction, defocus, absorption and a finite optical pupil can already change a real image.
A phase-contrast microscope images an illuminating annulus onto a phase plate ring near the objective's rear focal plane. The aligned ring attenuates and shifts direct light relative to most diffracted light; their interference changes image brightness.[ref]
The method is beautiful because the bright direct beam becomes its own reference: a small specimen-dependent complex amplitude can interfere with it and change the image at first order. Merely magnifying an invisible phase pattern would leave ∣t∣2 unchanged.

Phase-contrast microscope

Phase object

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Phase-contrast microscopy OurBigBook.com
A specimen whose leading optical effect is a spatially varying phase, rather than absorption. A thin specimen with refractive index ns​ in a medium of refractive index nm​ has, in a straight-path approximation,
ϕ(x,y)=λ2π​∫(ns​(x,y,z)−nm​)dz.
(27)
Here λ is the vacuum wavelength; the integral is an optical path length difference. For the chosen values λ=550nm, thickness 1μm and ns​−nm​=0.005, the phase is π/55≃0.0571 radians. This calculation does not identify thickness separately from refractive index contrast.[ref]
Weak phase object (t≃1+iϕ)
Words: 43
Phase object OurBigBook.com
A phase object for which the relevant relative phase variations are much smaller than one radian. The Taylor expansion eiϕ=1+iϕ+O(ϕ2) separates a direct reference term from a small specimen term. A constant overall phase can be removed before making this approximation: phase-contrast microscopy measures spatial variations, not an absolute common phase.

Phase plate

Words: 37
Phase-contrast microscopy OurBigBook.com
An optical filter that changes selected light's phase relative to other transmitted light. In phase-contrast microscopy, its ring can also attenuate the direct reference; the amplitude transmission and light intensity transmission must be distinguished. An amplitude transmission a=1/2 gives an intensity transmission a2=1/4.

Coherent zero-mode model of phase contrast

Words: 360
Phase-contrast microscopy OurBigBook.com
The following original model isolates the conversion mechanism. Use a periodic image window, unit illumination, ideal unit magnification, and a phase plate that changes only the zero spatial frequency. Write c0​=⟨eiϕ⟩ for the spatial mean. Multiplying that single Fourier coefficient by aeiθ, with 0<a≤1, gives the exact image field in this model:
Eout​=eiϕ+(aeiθ−1)c0​,Iout​=∣Eout​∣2.
(28)
This formula follows by splitting eiϕ=c0​+(eiϕ−c0​): the second term has zero mean and is left unchanged. A real annular, partly coherent instrument alters a finite band of directions, so this calculation is a mechanism model rather than its full image-formation law.
For a weak phase object with ⟨ϕ⟩=0, one has c0​=1+O(ϕ2) and hence
Eout​=aeiθ+iϕ+O(ϕ2),Iout​=a2+2aϕsinθ+O(ϕ2).​
(29)
The cross term is 2Re(ae−iθiϕ)=2aϕsinθ. Thus θ=π/2 makes positive ϕ brighter and θ=−π/2 makes it darker under this stated phase convention for complex amplitudes. The sign comes from this convention and chosen plate; a manufacturer’s positive/negative contrast labels should not be inferred from the sign of θ alone.
For example, choose a=0.5 and a zero-mean periodic pattern whose peak phase is 0.084. The first-order peak intensities are 0.25±0.084, compared with the uniform ideal bright-field microscopy value 1. The relative change about the reduced background is approximately 2ϕ/a for a quarter-cycle shift. Attenuating the reference increases relative contrast while reducing the background photon count; it is not light amplification or a universal improvement of signal-to-noise ratio.
Two checks expose what the model can and cannot measure. A spatially constant phase gives Eout​=aeiθeiϕ and Iout​=a2, so no absolute phase is recovered. Orthogonality of the constant and zero-mean parts also gives
⟨Iout​⟩=1−(1−a2)∣c0​∣2.
(30)
For a≤1 this cannot exceed the incident mean light intensity. The image redistributes brightness and loses some reference light rather than creating energy.

Phase-contrast image artifacts

Words: 43
Phase-contrast microscopy OurBigBook.com
A finite phase plate also intercepts diffracted light, altering low spatial frequencies. Halos and shade-off can therefore mimic borders or obscure interiors.[ref] In the coherent zero-mode model of phase contrast, the separation is perfect by assumption, so that model cannot predict those artifacts.

Zernike's discovery of phase contrast

Words: 132
Phase-contrast microscopy OurBigBook.com
Frits Zernike traced the idea to unwanted companion lines of a diffraction grating. Around 1930 he found that visible striping disappeared when a telescope focused exactly on the grating. A phase strip placed over the principal spectral line changed its relation to the companion light and restored contrast. He then applied the separation of direct and diffracted light to a microscope and demonstrated it at Zeiss in 1932.[ref]
His later absorbing and annular strips improved contrast and the appearance of halos; commercial Zeiss accessories followed in 1941.[ref] The route from a grating defect to biological observation illustrates why apparently unwanted instrumental effects can be productive experimental clues.

Fourier transform spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Multiplying a finite interferogram by a smooth window reduces sharp-edge artifacts. In the recovered radiation spectrum this convolves the true spectral density with the window's Fourier transform. Smoother windows generally lower sidelobes while broadening the main lobe, so a resolution figure must specify the window and criterion. Apodization does not recover unmeasured long-delay information.[ref]

Interferogram of an equally spaced spectral multiplet (∣g(1)∣=∣sin(NΔωτ/2)/[Nsin(Δωτ/2)]∣)

Words: 85
Fourier transform spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
For N equally intense spectral lines at ωn​=ω0​+nΔω, sum their delayed self-correlations as a geometric series. The result is
g(1)(τ)=e−i[ω0​+(N−1)Δω/2]τNsin(Δωτ/2)sin(NΔωτ/2)​.
(31)
The interferometric visibility revives every T=2π/Δω. There are N−1 zeros between adjacent revivals, at τ=jT/N for j=1,…,N−1. The removable singularity at a revival has unit modulus. Revival spacing fixes line spacing; the internal zero count fixes N under the equal-intensity model. The interferogram alone does not establish a fixed relative phase between the source lines or prove the emission is a coherent pulse train.

Fourier transform spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A Michelson interferometer mirror displacement x changes round-trip optical path difference by 2x, giving delay τ=2x/c. An interferogram recorded over a finite delay range is multiplied by a window; the recovered spectrum is the true spectrum convolved with that window's Fourier transform. Its characteristic frequency resolution scales inversely with delay range. Consequently a mirror travel range L gives δν∝c/L and δλ≃(λ2/c)δν∝λ2/L. Numerical width factors depend on the scan definition, window and resolution criterion; the inverse-travel scaling does not.

Optical fiber

Words: 2k Articles: 15
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
An optical fiber is a thin, flexible electromagnetic waveguide that carries light along its length. In a conventional step-index optical fiber, an optical fiber core with refractive index n1​ is surrounded by an optical fiber cladding with lower refractive index n2​. Suitable light rays remain confined by total internal reflection at this interface. The cladding is an optical part of the guide, distinct from its protective coating.[ref]
The useful surprise is that a transparent strand can deliver light around a route that a free beam would leave. This makes optical fibers useful for communications and for carrying collected light to a fiber-fed spectrograph. Guidance, successful launch, and surviving optical power are separate questions: the optical fiber acceptance angle constrains launch geometry, while optical fiber attenuation describes loss along the route.

Optical fiber purity and low-loss transmission

Words: 262
Optical fiber OurBigBook.com
Guiding light and retaining useful optical power are different achievements. Charles Kuen Kao and George Alfred Hockham argued that impurities need not impose the measured losses of existing glasses on every future optical fiber. Their 1966 paper treats wave absorption, scattering of light and guidance separately; reducing impurity absorption leaves intrinsic material losses and geometric losses to address. This was a route toward practical communication, building on existing optical fibers, rather than the invention of every use of guided light.[ref]
The launch experiment used clad glass optical fibers fixed in capillary tubes with epoxy for end polishing. Laser illumination gave transverse normal mode patterns; input-spot displacement and polarization of an electromagnetic wave controlled excitation. These observations tested guidance, not kilometre-scale optical fiber attenuation.[ref]
Charles Kuen Kao's lecture describes the complementary material experiment: short, polished glass samples, including plasma-deposited fused silicon dioxide, were examined with purpose-built single-beam and later double-beam spectrophotometers. A separate ellipsometry measurement assessed end-surface specular reflection, a check against confusing interface loss with bulk wave absorption. The readout was loss versus wavelength. Comparing glass samples supported impurity reduction as a route to lower loss. Surface contamination and the tiny bulk loss of short samples limited inference; the result did not itself demonstrate a long drawn optical fiber. The lecture also credits subsequent manufacturing work at Corning.[ref]
An original scale comparison makes the material problem tangible. In the uniform optical fiber attenuation model, a stipulated 20dB/km leaves 10−2=0.01 of launched optical power after 1km; a stipulated 0.2dB/km leaves 10−0.02≃0.95499. Both guides could satisfy the same total internal reflection condition. A successful spot pattern at the output therefore cannot by itself establish a useful communication distance.

Step-index optical fiber

Words: 507 Articles: 3
Optical fiber OurBigBook.com
A step-index optical fiber has a nearly uniform refractive index n1​ throughout its optical fiber core, with an abrupt decrease to n2​<n1​ in its optical fiber cladding. In a straight, ideal guide, meridional rays stay in a plane containing the optical axis and trace a zigzag through repeated total internal reflection. This is a geometrical optics approximation; it is particularly useful for a multimode optical fiber whose core diameter is large compared with the wavelength.
The upper panel shows an accepted meridional ray; the lower panel enlarges the limiting geometry. The angle of incidence i at the side wall is measured from its normal vector, whereas the internal ray angle ϕ and external launch angle θ are measured from the optical axis. Thus i+ϕ=90∘. The limiting ray is a boundary of the ideal model, rather than a complete normal mode solution.

Step-index fiber normalized frequency (V=2πan12​−n22​​/λ0​)

Words: 46
Step-index optical fiber OurBigBook.com
The dimensionless waveguide parameter V combines radius, vacuum wavelength and the numerical aperture factor. In the weak-guidance scalar model the first additional spatial family appears at V=j0,1​=2.404825…, the first positive zero of a Bessel function of the first kind. The fundamental family has no positive cutoff. Its two polarizations are not two distinct spatial profiles.

Meridional ray bend threshold (Rc​=n2​r/(n1​cosβ−n2​))

Words: 77
Step-index optical fiber OurBigBook.com
For a light ray launched on the centreline in the plane of a circular optical fiber bend, let R be centreline radius, r core radius and β the internal launch angle from the tangent. The straight segment's distance from the bend centre is Rcosβ. Thus its outer-wall angle of incidence satisfies sini=Rcosβ/(R+r). Equating this to n2​/n1​ gives the limiting total internal reflection threshold in the title, provided n1​cosβ>n2​. Radially displaced or nonplanar launches need different geometry; this is not a universal wave-optical loss cutoff.

Optical fiber acceptance angle (θmax​)

Words: 260
Step-index optical fiber OurBigBook.com
The optical fiber acceptance angle is the largest launch half-angle admitted by the specified guide model. For a flat entrance face perpendicular to the optical axis, external refractive index n0​, and a straight step-index optical fiber, Snell's law at the entrance gives
n0​sinθ=n1​sinϕ.
(32)
At the core–cladding interface, the critical angle for total internal reflection ic​ satisfies
sinic​=n1​n2​​,i=2π​−ϕ.
(33)
For a meridional ray, strict total internal reflection requires i>ic​. At the limiting geometry i=ic​, the refracted light ray is tangent to the interface, so
n0​sinθmax​=n1​cosic​=n12​−n22​​≡NA.
(34)
This identifies the numerical aperture with an entrance cone under these assumptions. With n0​=1 for air, the conventional inclusive boundary condition is
sinθ≤n12​−n22​​,
(35)
for a nonnegative launch angle θ; a practical launch stays inside the boundary. If NA>n0​, this ideal model imposes no further restriction within the forward hemisphere, and arcsin(NA/n0​) must not be used. The light ray must also intersect the optical fiber core: a suitable angle alone does not correct a misplaced beam.
For an original example, take n1​=1.50, n2​=1.48 and air at the entrance. Then
NA=2.25−2.1904​=0.0596​≃0.244131,θmax​=arcsin(0.244131)≃14.13∘.
(36)
The internal limiting angle is only ϕmax​≃9.37∘, while the critical angle for total internal reflection is ic​≃80.63∘. A 10∘ launch has ϕ≃6.65∘ and i≃83.35∘, so it satisfies total internal reflection. A 20∘ launch has ϕ≃13.18∘ and i≃76.82∘, so it fails this test.
This cone is a geometrical optics result for meridional rays. A single-mode optical fiber requires the spatial overlap of the incident electromagnetic wave with its guided normal mode; its numerical aperture does not impose an exact angular cutoff on arbitrary beams. Diffraction, finite cladding, and bends require a physical optics description.[ref]

Single-mode optical fiber

Words: 62
Optical fiber OurBigBook.com
A single-mode optical fiber supports only its fundamental spatial guided normal mode at the operating wavelength, with possible distinct states of polarization of an electromagnetic wave. The designation must include wavelength: MIT's fibre laboratory explicitly notes that a fibre sold for single-mode operation can support several normal modes at its helium–neon laser wavelength.[ref]

Graded-index optical fiber

Words: 69
Optical fiber OurBigBook.com
A graded-index optical fiber has an optical fiber core whose refractive index varies smoothly with distance from the optical axis. Refraction bends light rays through the varying medium; the straight zigzag of a step-index optical fiber no longer describes their paths. The local launch cone can depend on entry position.[ref]

Optical fiber coupling and bend experiment

Words: 160
Optical fiber OurBigBook.com
MIT's Optical Waveguides and Fibers, Laboratory Exercise No. 7 (Fall 2005), describes a teaching apparatus. A cleaned, flat-ended multimode optical fiber receives helium–neon laser light through a microscope objective optical lens; a micropositioner aligns the input. The launch deliberately overfills the fibre's cone. A beam splitter sends a sample to a reference photodetector to track laser fluctuations. The fixed output faces a screen or a photodetector on a rotation stage with angular measurement calibration. Readings every two degrees, divided by simultaneous reference readings, give an angular profile. Repeating with an underfilled launch is a control: too few excited normal modes underestimate numerical aperture. Optional index-matching fluid removes cladding-carried light. Bending the fibre reveals leakage and reduced output on an oscilloscope. The handout supplies no measured trace or absolute detector measurement calibration, and this angular scan does not determine loss per kilometre.[ref]

Optical fiber attenuation (αdB​)

Words: 570 Articles: 1
Optical fiber OurBigBook.com
Optical fiber attenuation is the reduction of transmitted optical power along an optical fiber. Define a positive loss in decibels by comparing optical power P(0) already launched into the guide with surviving optical power P(z):
A(z)=10log10​(P(z)P(0)​)dB.
(37)
The factor ten applies to a power ratio; the factor twenty applies to a wave amplitude ratio only when power is proportional to its square under the same conditions.[ref]
For a uniform illustrative model with constant loss coefficient αdB​ in dB/km and distance z in kilometres,
A(z)=αdB​z,P(0)P(z)​=10−A(z)/(10dB).
(38)
For αdB​=0.2dB/km over 10km, the loss is 2dB and
P(0)P(10km)​=10−0.2≃0.630957.
(39)
Thus about 63.1% of the launched optical power survives and 36.9% is lost. This is an illustrative coefficient, not a property of all optical fibers, and is independent of the earlier illustrative refractive indices.
The exponential decay follows from assuming each equal distance interval transmits the same fraction. For two such intervals, power ratios multiply; their logarithms add, so the losses in decibels add. Two 5km sections each transmit 10−0.1≃0.794328; together they transmit (0.794328)2≃0.630957. The loss curve is straight in decibels and curved on a linear power scale.
Wave absorption and scattering of light can remove guided optical power even in a straight fibre, while bends can let it escape. Entrance losses, joints and connectors contribute additional losses; they belong separately from a uniform distance coefficient. This is why a measured end-to-end power ratio need not equal the straight-fibre model.[ref]

Optical fiber cutback measurement (αdB​=10log10​(Ps​/Pℓ​)/(Lℓ​−Ls​))

Words: 309
Optical fiber attenuation OurBigBook.com
An optical fiber cutback measurement estimates distributed optical fiber attenuation by comparing a long guide with the short input portion left after cutting the output end back. Keep the launch untouched. For the following original functional model, fix wavelength, source output, input alignment and collected output cone; subtract a dark reading and keep the photodetector in its linear range. Renewed end-face quality and changed normal mode populations can still spoil the comparison. The diagram describes a measurement principle, not Kao's historical short-glass apparatus.
Let Lℓ​>Ls​ be lengths in kilometres, Pℓ​,Ps​ the corresponding positive dark-subtracted readings, and C the same launch and detection factor. A uniform guide obeys
Pℓ​=C10−αdB​Lℓ​/10,Ps​=C10−αdB​Ls​/10,αdB​=Lℓ​−Ls​10​log10​Pℓ​Ps​​.
(40)
Here αdB​ and its estimate are numerical values in dB/km. Dividing eliminates C; taking a logarithm proves the formula. A changed C instead adds an error 10log10​(Cs​/Cℓ​)/(Lℓ​−Ls​). Reconnecting the launch between readings defeats this cancellation.
For original chosen values Ls​=0.1km, Lℓ​=2.1km, Ps​=100μW and αdB​=0.5dB/km, the predicted long reading is Pℓ​=10010−0.1≃79.4328μW. The ratio gives 1dB for the removed 2km and hence 0.5dB/km.
Suppose an unremoved additive detector background contributes b=5μW to both readings. Then the apparent coefficient is
αdB​=210​log10​79.4328+5100+5​≃0.47339dB/km.
(41)
This is a bias of an estimator: a common additive background pushes the ratio toward one, whereas a common multiplicative factor cancels. For independent small zero-mean errors with standard deviations σs​,σℓ​ on the dark-subtracted readings, a first-order Taylor expansion gives
σα​≃(Lℓ​−Ls​)ln1010​(Ps​σs​​)2+(Pℓ​σℓ​​)2​.
(42)
Choosing both standard deviations as 1μW gives σα​≃0.03491dB/km. A shared estimated dark offset introduces covariance, so it requires a different uncertainty calculation. Near zero signal, the logarithm and this linear approximation become unreliable.

Focal-ratio degradation is the broadening of the output angular cone of an optical fiber relative to its input cone. It can make a spectrograph collimator lose transmitted light or require larger optics. Stress, bends, and mode mixing in the fiber can contribute.

The central guiding region of a conventional optical fiber; in a step-index optical fiber, its refractive index exceeds that of the surrounding optical fiber cladding.

The optical material surrounding the optical fiber core. In a conventional step-index optical fiber, its lower refractive index permits total internal reflection; it is distinct from the protective coating.

Adaptive optics

Words: 306 Articles: 8
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
Adaptive optics measures changing wavefront errors and corrects them using a deformable mirror. A wavefront sensor supplies measurements to a fast feedback controller; a guide star provides the reference. It improves astronomical seeing toward diffraction-limited resolution.

Deformable mirror

Words: 164 Articles: 2
Adaptive optics OurBigBook.com
A deformable mirror changes its optical surface using an array of actuators. For reflection near normal incidence, surface displacement changes optical path length by twice that displacement.

Deformable-mirror Fourier-mode counting

Words: 92
Deformable mirror OurBigBook.com
For actuator pitch D/N, full-cycle spatial frequency components are limited to N/2 by sampling. Integer lattice counting in a circular frequency disk gives approximately πN2/4 signed points; conjugate pairing halves the number of pairs, and two real wave phase quadratures per pair restore approximately πN2/4 real coefficients. Counting only positive-quadrant frequency representatives gives πN2/16, but it omits other orientations or quadratures unless a restricted convention is specified. Area approximations have boundary corrections and do not give exact integer ranks. A square sampling cutoff and a circular illuminated actuator footprint are distinct geometric restrictions.

Deformable-mirror control radius (θmax​=Nλ/(2D))

Words: 48
Deformable mirror OurBigBook.com
With N actuators across diameter D, the projected pitch is approximately D/N. The Nyquist spatial frequency is N/(2D), so the largest correctable angular speckle displacement along an actuator row is Nλ/(2D). A square actuator array gives a square ideal spatial-frequency region. See the Bordé–Traub wavefront-control derivation.

Adaptive-optics sky coverage is the fraction of targets for which a sufficiently bright nearby guide star allows useful correction. A monochromator selects a narrow, adjustable wavelength interval from an optical spectrum. Its finite spectral bandwidth matters when calibrating a photodetector's spectral responsivity in calibrated radiant-flux measurement.

An optical power meter measures collected radiant flux using a calibrated detector and readout. With a photodiode, its conversion to watts depends on spectral responsivity, as in calibrated radiant-flux measurement.

Optical instrument OurBigBook.com

Single-photon detector

Words: 113 Articles: 1
Photodetector OurBigBook.com
A photodetector capable of registering an individual absorbed photon as a distinguishable event. The detection record may include a click time and an output-channel label. Such a detector need not resolve the number of photons in a pulse: an ordinary single-pixel single-photon avalanche diode produces essentially the same saturated avalanche pulse when one or several photons trigger the same detection interval. Detector efficiency, dark counts and detector dead time affect the observed photon counting statistics.

Dark count (rdark​)

Words: 52
Single-photon detector OurBigBook.com
A registered detector event occurring without an incident signal photon. For a single-photon avalanche diode, internally generated carriers can trigger the same avalanche as an absorbed photon. The dark-count rate rdark​ is the mean number of these events per unit time under specified operating conditions. Such events can contaminate coincidence counting and increase the quantum bit error rate in quantum key distribution.
